evidence.text: Acclimatisation societies were voluntary associations in the 19th and 20th centuries that encouraged the introduction of non-native species in various places around the world with the hope of their acclimatisation and adaptation.
evidence.title: Acclimatisation society

evidence.text: The motivation at the time was a sense that introducing these species of plants and animals would enrich the flora and fauna of a region .
evidence.title: Acclimatisation society

evidence.text: These societies were born during a period of colonialism when Europeans began to settle in unfamiliar environments, and the movement sought to establish familiar plants and animals (mainly from Europe) in new areas while also bringing exotic and useful foreign plants and animals into the European centres.
evidence.title: Acclimatisation society

evidence.text: Today it is widely understood that introducing species can be harmful to native species and their ecosystems; for example, in Australia plants were harmed by rabbits' overgrazing; in North America house sparrows displace and kill native birds; and around the world, salamander populations are today threatened by introduced fungal infections.
evidence.title: Acclimatisation society

evidence.text: At the time of acclimatisation societies, however, this was insufficiently understood .
evidence.title: Acclimatisation society

evidence.text: The prohibition "do not feed the animals" reflects a policy forbidding the artificial feeding of wildlife (wild or feral animals) in situations where the animals, or the people doing the feeding, might be harmed.
evidence.title: Do not feed the animals

evidence.text: Signs displaying this message are commonly found in zoos, circuses, animal theme parks, aquariums, national parks, parks, public spaces, farms, and other places where people come into contact with wildlife.
evidence.title: Do not feed the animals

evidence.text: In some cases there are laws to enforce such no-feeding policies.
evidence.title: Do not feed the animals

evidence.text: However, some people (such as some of those who enjoy feeding pigeons in cities) openly and strongly oppose such laws claiming that animals such as pigeons can be an amenity for people who do not have company such as friends or family, and say that the laws prohibiting feeding animals in urban places must change.
evidence.title: Do not feed the animals

evidence.text: In some countries, such as Greece, feeding the pigeons in cities is a widespread practice.
evidence.title: Do not feed the animals

evidence.text: Cultural hostility to feeding animals in cities and laws that ban the practice raise concerns about how humans relate to other living beings in the urban environment.
evidence.title: Do not feed the animals

evidence.text: Politicians have also protested laws that ban feeding feral pigeons in cities.
evidence.title: Do not feed the animals

evidence.text: Feral pigeons in cities existed for thousands of years but only recently in some countries humans started seeing them as a nuisance and became hostile to them.
evidence.title: Do not feed the animals

evidence.text: In India, feeding feral animals in cities is considered a noble act.
evidence.title: Do not feed the animals

evidence.text: Academicians say that how humans treat animals is related to how humans treat each other and thus raise concerns about the cultural shift from seeing feral city pigeons as harmless in the 1800s to seeing them a undesirable in some countries in the 2000s.
evidence.title: Do not feed the animals

evidence.text: The Rochester Mustangs were an American junior A ice hockey team that was located in Rochester, Minnesota.

evidence.text: The Mustangs were in existence from 1986 to 2002.
evidence.title: Rochester Mustangs (junior)

evidence.text: Prior to 1986, the organization was located in Austin, Minnesota, and was known as the Austin Mavericks.

evidence.text: The Mavericks played from 1974 until 1977 in the Midwest Junior Hockey League, before moving to the United States Hockey League in 1978.

evidence.text: It was designed by John T. Windrim and built in 1926-1927.

evidence.text: Banneker Recreation Center is an historic structure located in the Columbia Heights neighborhood of Washington, D.C. The building was built in 1934 and was named for Benjamin Banneker, a free African American who assisted in the survey of boundaries of the original District of Columba in 1791.

evidence.text: It was known as a premier African American recreation center in the city.
evidence.title: Banneker Recreation Center

evidence.text: It was listed on the District of Columbia Inventory of Historic Sites in 1985 and it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1986.
evidence.title: Banneker Recreation Center

evidence.text: The structure currently houses the Banneker Community Center, a unit of the District of Columbia Department of Parks and Recreation.
evidence.title: Banneker Recreation Center

evidence.text: Edward S. Stephens (c. 1849 – September 30, 1909) was an educator in the United States in the late 19th century.
evidence.title: Edward S. Stephens

evidence.text: He was the first principal of the Catholic Hill School, the first public school for African Americans in Asheville, North Carolina.
evidence.title: Edward S. Stephens

evidence.text: During his time in Asheville, Stephens and other prominent African American citizens, with the support of heir and philanthropist George Washington Vanderbilt II, established the Young Men's Institute, modeled after the Young Men's Christian Association.
evidence.title: Edward S. Stephens

evidence.text: Asheville's noted Stephens-Lee High School (now Stephens-Lee Recreation Center), the successor to the Catholic Hill School, which burned down in 1917, was partially named after Stephens.
evidence.title: Edward S. Stephens

evidence.text: Payne's Cemetery was a 13 acre cemetery located in the Benning Ridge neighborhood of Washington, D.C., in the United States.
evidence.title: Payne's Cemetery

evidence.text: It was founded in 1851 as a privately owned secular cemetery open to the public, but it primarily served the city's African American community.
evidence.title: Payne's Cemetery

evidence.text: The cemetery was declared abandoned by the city in 1966.
evidence.title: Payne's Cemetery

evidence.text: About 2,000 bodies at Payne's Cemetery were reinterred at National Harmony Memorial Park cemetery in Prince George's County, Maryland.
evidence.title: Payne's Cemetery

evidence.text: Two public schools and a recreation center were constructed atop the cemetery in the late 1960s, during which time hundreds of corpses were unearthed and summarily disposed of.
evidence.title: Payne's Cemetery

evidence.text: The Davis Avenue Recreation Center is a historic recreation facility in Mobile, Alabama.
evidence.title: Davis Avenue Recreation Center

evidence.text: The facility was established in 1921 as the first public leisure center for African Americans in segregated Mobile.
evidence.title: Davis Avenue Recreation Center

evidence.text: Initially known as the Davis Avenue Community House, it also featured tennis courts, a swimming pool, and a small park.
evidence.title: Davis Avenue Recreation Center

evidence.text: The need for a larger facility was soon realized, and in 1936 the current structure was completed.
evidence.title: Davis Avenue Recreation Center

evidence.text: It was the only public recreation facility in Mobile built using Works Progress Administration funds.
evidence.title: Davis Avenue Recreation Center

evidence.text: It was added to the National Register of Historic Places on June 27, 2011, due to its significance to the African American history in the city.
evidence.title: Davis Avenue Recreation Center

evidence.text: Songs From The Trees (A Musical Memoir Collection) is singer-songwriter Carly Simon's sixth greatest-hits album.

evidence.text: The Quiet American is a 1955 novel by English author Graham Greene which depicts French colonialism in Vietnam being uprooted by the Americans during the 1950s.
evidence.title: The Quiet American

evidence.text: The novel implicitly questions the foundations of growing American involvement in Vietnam in the 1950s and is unique in its exploration of the subject topic through the links among its three main characters - Fowler, Pyle and Phuong.
evidence.title: The Quiet American

evidence.text: The novel has received much attention due to its prediction of the outcome of the Vietnam War and subsequent American foreign policy since the 1950s.
evidence.title: The Quiet American

evidence.text: Graham Greene portrays a U.S. official named Pyle as so blinded by American exceptionalism that he cannot see the calamities he brings upon the Vietnamese.
evidence.title: The Quiet American

evidence.text: It was adapted as two different movies during 1958 and 2002.
evidence.title: The Quiet American

evidence.text: The book uses Greene's experiences as a war correspondent for "The Times" and "Le Figaro" in French Indochina 1951–1954.
evidence.title: The Quiet American

evidence.text: He was apparently inspired to write "The Quiet American" during October 1951 while driving back to Saigon from Ben Tre province.
evidence.title: The Quiet American

evidence.text: He was accompanied by an American aid worker who lectured him about finding a "third force in Vietnam” .
evidence.title: The Quiet American

evidence.text: Audie Murphy (20 June 1925 – 28 May 1971) was a highly decorated American soldier and Medal of Honor recipient who turned actor.
evidence.title: Film career of Audie Murphy

evidence.text: He portrayed himself in the film ""To Hell and Back"", the account of his World War II experiences.
evidence.title: Film career of Audie Murphy

evidence.text: During the 1950s and 1960s he was cast primarily in westerns.
evidence.title: Film career of Audie Murphy

evidence.text: While often the hero, he proved his ability to portray a cold-blooded hired gun in "No Name on the Bullet".
evidence.title: Film career of Audie Murphy

evidence.text: A notable exception to the westerns was "The Quiet American" in which he co-starred with Michael Redgrave.
evidence.title: Film career of Audie Murphy

evidence.text: Murphy made over 40 feature films and often worked with directors more than once.
evidence.title: Film career of Audie Murphy

evidence.text: Jesse Hibbs who directed "To Hell and Back" worked with the star on six films, only half of which were westerns.

evidence.text: The Philisteins were a garage punk band formed in Hobart in 1985 as The Cheesemongers with a line-up including Scott Harrison on bass guitar; Aydn Hibberd on guitar, vocals and harmonica; and Guy Lucas on guitar, vocals and organ.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: In 1986 Konrad Park joined on drums and they adopted a new name, The Philisteins.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: In 1987 they issued their debut album, "Reverberations", and soon after relocated to Adelaide and signed with local label, Greasy Pop Records.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: In December 1988 they released an eight-track extended play, "Bloody Convicts", with Harrison replaced by Ian Wettenhall on bass guitar and Nick Bruer on drums.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: They followed with a six-track EP, "Some Kind of Philisteins", in November 1989, with Bruer replaced by Stewart Tabert.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: Their full-length album, "Lifestyles of the Wretched and Forgettable", appeared in November of the next year on Dog Meat Records and they had moved to Melbourne.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: By 1992 they disbanded and Lucas, Tabert and Wettenhall formed another group, The Freeloaders.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: Hibberd was a founding member of indie rock band, Powder Monkeys.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: In March 1998 Guy Lucas died of a drug overdose.

evidence.text: A compilation album, "A Savage Affection: 1986–1992", appeared in December 2007.

evidence.text: The Philisteins were a garage punk band formed in Hobart in 1985 as The Cheesemongers with a line-up including Scott Harrison on bass guitar; Aydn Hibberd on guitar, vocals and harmonica; and Guy Lucas on guitar, vocals and organ.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: In 1986 Konrad Park joined on drums and they adopted a new name, The Philisteins.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: In 1987 they issued their debut album, "Reverberations", and soon after relocated to Adelaide and signed with local label, Greasy Pop Records.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: In December 1988 they released an eight-track extended play, "Bloody Convicts", with Harrison replaced by Ian Wettenhall on bass guitar and Nick Bruer on drums.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: They followed with a six-track EP, "Some Kind of Philisteins", in November 1989, with Bruer replaced by Stewart Tabert.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: Their full-length album, "Lifestyles of the Wretched and Forgettable", appeared in November of the next year on Dog Meat Records and they had moved to Melbourne.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: By 1992 they disbanded and Lucas, Tabert and Wettenhall formed another group, The Freeloaders.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: Hibberd was a founding member of indie rock band, Powder Monkeys.
evidence.title: The Philisteins

evidence.text: In March 1998 Guy Lucas died of a drug overdose.

evidence.text: The Palm Canyon Times was a bi-weekly newspaper and magazine primarily for Palm Springs, California and the adjoining cities in Palm Springs areas of the Coachella Valley.

evidence.text: "Ode to the Confederate Dead" is a long poem by the American poet-critic Allen Tate published in 1928 in Tate's first book of poems, "Mr. Pope and Other Poems".
evidence.title: Ode to the Confederate Dead

evidence.text: It is one of Tate's best-known poems and considered by some critics to be his most "important."
evidence.title: Ode to the Confederate Dead

evidence.text: Heavily influenced by the work of T. S. Eliot, this Modernist poem takes place in a graveyard in the South where the narrator grieves the loss of the Confederate soldiers buried there.
evidence.title: Ode to the Confederate Dead

evidence.text: However, unlike the "" to the Confederate Dead written by the 19th-century American poet Henry Timrod, Tate's "Ode" is not a straightforward ode.
evidence.title: Ode to the Confederate Dead

evidence.text: Instead, Tate uses the graveyard and the dead Confederate soldiers as a metaphor for his narrator's troubled state of mind, and the poem charts the narrator's dark stream of consciousness, as he contemplates (or tries to avoid contemplating) his own mortality.
evidence.title: Ode to the Confederate Dead

evidence.text: The Great Falls Tectonic Zone is a major intracontinental shear zone between the Hearne craton and Wyoming craton basement rock of the Archean Eon which form part of the North American continent.

evidence.text: It is named for the Great Falls of the Missouri River, a major geologic feature of the area.

evidence.text: The central part of the zone lacks Archean rock, however, leading at least one group of scientists to speculate that it was formed very late in the Paleoproterozoic Era.
evidence.title: Great Falls Tectonic Zone

evidence.text: The Bransfield Basin is a back-arc rift basin located off the Northern tip of the Antarctic Peninsula.
evidence.title: Bransfield Basin

evidence.text: The basin lies within a Northeast and Southwest trending strait that separates the peninsula from the nearby South Shetland Islands to the Northwest.
evidence.title: Bransfield Basin

evidence.text: The basin extends for more than 500 km from Smith Island (South Shetland Islands) to a portion of the Hero Fracture Zone.
evidence.title: Bransfield Basin

evidence.text: The basin can be subdivided into three basins: Western, Central, and Eastern.
evidence.title: Bransfield Basin

evidence.text: The Western basin is 130 km long by 70 km wide with a depth of 1.3 km , the Central basin is 230 km long by 60 km wide with a depth of 1.9 km , and the Eastern basin is 150 km long by 40 km wide with a depth of over 2.7 km .
evidence.title: Bransfield Basin

evidence.text: The three basins are separated by the Deception Island and Bridgeman Island.
evidence.title: Bransfield Basin

evidence.text: The moho depth in the region has been seismically interpreted to be roughly 34 km deep.
evidence.title: Bransfield Basin

evidence.text: Oscar is a British TV serial first transmitted by BBC 2 in March 1985.
evidence.title: Oscar (TV serial)

evidence.text: Michael Gambon portrayed Oscar Wilde while other actors included Robin Lermitte as Lord Alfred Douglas, Tim Hardy as Alfred Taylor, Emily Richard as Constance Wilde and Norman Rodway as the Marquis of Queensberry.
evidence.title: Oscar (TV serial)

evidence.text: The serial concentrated on Wilde's trials and time in prison.
evidence.title: Oscar (TV serial)

evidence.text: The play Oscar Wilde, written by Leslie and Sewell Stokes, is based on the life of the Irish playwright Oscar Wilde in which Wilde's friend, the controversial author and journalist Frank Harris, appears as a character.
evidence.title: Oscar Wilde (play)

evidence.text: The play, which contains much of Wilde's actual writings, starts with Wilde's literary success and his friendship with Lord Alfred Douglas, turns into a courtroom melodrama, and ends with Wilde as a broken alcoholic after two years in prison.
evidence.title: Oscar Wilde (play)

evidence.text: Harold Sherwood Spencer (born 1890, date of death unknown) was an American-born British anti-homosexuality and antisemitic activist during and after World War I.
evidence.title: Harold Sherwood Spencer

evidence.text: He was closely associated with Noel Pemberton Billing and Lord Alfred Douglas.
evidence.title: Harold Sherwood Spencer

evidence.text: Lord Alfred Bruce Douglas (22 October 187020 March 1945), nicknamed Bosie, was a British author, poet, translator, and political commentator, better known as the friend and lover of Oscar Wilde.
evidence.title: Lord Alfred Douglas

evidence.text: Much of his early poetry was Uranian in theme, though he tended, later in life, to distance himself from both Wilde's influence and his own role as a Uranian poet.
evidence.title: Lord Alfred Douglas

evidence.text: Politically he would describe himself as "a strong Conservative of the 'Diehard' variety".
evidence.title: Lord Alfred Douglas

evidence.text: Salome's Last Dance is a 1988 film by British film director, Ken Russell.
evidence.title: Salome's Last Dance

evidence.text: Although most of the action is a verbatim performance of Oscar Wilde's 1893 play "Salome", which is itself based on a story from the New Testament, there is also a framing narrative written by Russell himself.
evidence.title: Salome's Last Dance

evidence.text: Wilde (Nickolas Grace) and his lover Lord Alfred Douglas (Douglas Hodge) arrive late on Guy Fawkes Day at their friend's brothel, where they are treated to a surprise staging of Wilde's play, public performances of which have just been banned in England by the Lord Chamberlain's office.
evidence.title: Salome's Last Dance

evidence.text: John Francis Bloxam (1873 – 1928) was an English Uranian author and churchman.
evidence.title: John Francis Bloxam

evidence.text: Bloxam was an undergraduate at Exeter College, Oxford when his story, "the Priest and the Acolyte", appeared in the sole issue of "the Chameleon: a Bazaar of Dangerous and Smiling Chances", a periodical which he also served as editor.
evidence.title: John Francis Bloxam

evidence.text: The story details the love affair of a priest and his lover, a boy.
evidence.title: John Francis Bloxam

evidence.text: The affair, when discovered, triggers the priest's suicide.
evidence.title: John Francis Bloxam

evidence.text: A poem, "A Summer Hour", also with pederastic themes, appeared in "the Artist".
evidence.title: John Francis Bloxam

evidence.text: The contents of "the Chameleon", which also included Lord Alfred Douglas' notorious poem "Two Loves", would be used against Oscar Wilde in his trial.
evidence.title: John Francis Bloxam

evidence.text: Bloxam was a convert to Anglo-Catholicism, and became a priest.
evidence.title: John Francis Bloxam

evidence.title: De Profundis (letter)

evidence.title: The Judas Kiss (play)

evidence.text: Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde (16 October 185430 November 1900) was a prolific Irish writer who wrote plays, fiction, essays, and poetry.
evidence.title: Oscar Wilde

evidence.text: After writing in different forms throughout the 1880s, he became one of London's most popular playwrights in the early 1890s.
evidence.title: Oscar Wilde

evidence.text: He is best remembered for his epigrams and plays, the novel "The Picture of Dorian Gray", as well as the circumstances of his imprisonment and early death.
evidence.title: Oscar Wilde

evidence.text: He is known for his one-man show, "Oscar Remembered", which tells the story of the Irish playwright Oscar Wilde as seen from the perspective of his lover and nemesis, Lord Alfred Douglas.

evidence.text: The Timex Sinclair 1000 (TS1000) was the first computer produced by Timex Sinclair, a joint venture between Timex Corporation and Sinclair Research.
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair 1000

evidence.text: It was launched in July 1982, with a US sales price of US$99.95, making it the cheapest home computer to date; it was advertised as "the first computer under $100".
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair 1000

evidence.text: The computer was aimed at regular home users.
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair 1000

evidence.text: Unlike earlier computers aimed at home users, the TS1000 was not a kit which had to be soldered and assembled.
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair 1000

evidence.text: As purchased, the TS1000 was fully assembled and ready to be plugged into the users' home TV (which served as a video monitor).
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair 1000

evidence.text: The TS1000 was a slightly-modified version of the Sinclair ZX81 with an NTSC RF modulator, designed for use with North American TVs, instead of the UK PAL RF modulator which was used for units sold in Portugal.
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair 1000

evidence.text: The TS1000 doubled the onboard RAM from 1 KB to 2 KB.
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair 1000

evidence.text: The TS1000's casing had slightly more internal shielding but remained the same as Sinclair's, including the membrane keyboard.
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair 1000

evidence.text: It had black-and-white graphics and no sound.
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair 1000

evidence.text: It was followed by an improved version, the Timex Sinclair 1500 which had substantially more RAM (16 KB) and a lower price (US$80).
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair 1000

evidence.text: However, the TS1500 did not achieve market success, given that the marketplace was by this time dominated by Commodore, RadioShack, Atari and Apple.
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair 1000

evidence.text: The Wave Mate Bullet was a Z80 single-board computer from the late 1970s and early 1980s which used the CP/M operating system.
evidence.title: Wave Mate Bullet

evidence.text: This computer is rarely seen now but has historical value as an early microcomputer pioneer.
evidence.title: Wave Mate Bullet

evidence.text: It was sold in Australia, the United States and Europe and was apparently popular in academic settings.
evidence.title: Wave Mate Bullet

evidence.text: Tony Tebby is probably most famous for designing Qdos, the computer operating system used in the Sinclair QL personal computer, whilst working as an engineer at Sinclair Research in the early 1980s.
evidence.title: Tony Tebby

evidence.text: He left Sinclair Research in 1984 in protest at the premature launch of the QL, and formed QJUMP Ltd., a software house specializing in system software and utilities for the QL, based in Rampton, Cambridgeshire, England.
evidence.title: Tony Tebby

evidence.text: Sinclair Research Ltd is a British consumer electronics company founded by Clive Sinclair in Cambridge.
evidence.title: Sinclair Research

evidence.text: It was originally incorporated in 1973 as Westminster Mail Order Ltd, renamed Sinclair Instrument Ltd, then Science of Cambridge Ltd, then Sinclair Computers Ltd, and finally Sinclair Research Ltd in 1975.
evidence.title: Sinclair Research

evidence.text: It remained dormant until 1976, when it was activated with the intention of continuing Sinclair's commercial work from his earlier company Sinclair Radionics, and adopted the name Sinclair Research in 1981.
evidence.title: Sinclair Research

evidence.text: The ZX81 is a home computer produced by Sinclair Research and manufactured in Scotland by Timex Corporation.
evidence.title: ZX81

evidence.text: It was launched in the United Kingdom in March 1981 as the successor to Sinclair's ZX80 and was designed to be a low-cost introduction to home computing for the general public.
evidence.title: ZX81

evidence.text: It was hugely successful, and more than 1.5 million units were sold before it was discontinued.
evidence.title: ZX81

evidence.text: The ZX81 found commercial success in many other countries, notably the United States, where it was initially sold as the ZX-81.
evidence.title: ZX81

evidence.text: Timex manufactured and distributed it under licence and enjoyed a substantial but brief boom in sales.
evidence.title: ZX81

evidence.text: Timex later produced its own versions of the ZX81 for the US market – the Timex Sinclair 1000 and Timex Sinclair 1500.
evidence.title: ZX81

evidence.text: Unauthorised clones of the ZX81 were produced in several countries.
evidence.title: ZX81

evidence.text: Jim Westwood was the chief engineer at Sinclair Research Ltd in the 1980s, starting at the company in 1963.
evidence.title: Jim Westwood

evidence.text: Westwood was the technical mastermind behind many of Sinclair's products and worked there for more than twenty years.
evidence.title: Jim Westwood

evidence.text: Sir Clive Sinclair and Westwood shared a connection even before they met when Westwood had previously worked at an electronics store in London which was owned by Bernard Babani, Sinclair's publisher.
evidence.title: Jim Westwood

evidence.text: This gave Westwood a good degree of familiarity with Sinclair's designs, which prompted him to join Sinclair's fledgling company, Sinclair Radionics.
evidence.title: Jim Westwood

evidence.text: Westwood subsequently had a hand in most of the company's products, including the calculators, audio equipment, ZX Spectrum computers and TV80.
evidence.title: Jim Westwood

evidence.text: He is still designing hardware for Amino Communications, and is a partner in Cambridge Electronics Consultancy.
evidence.title: Jim Westwood

evidence.text: Timex Sinclair was a joint venture between the British company Sinclair Research and Timex Corporation in an effort to gain an entry into the rapidly growing early-1980s home computer market in North America.
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair

evidence.text: The choice of partnership was natural, as Timex was already the main contractor for manufacture of Sinclair's ZX81 and ZX Spectrum computers at its Scottish plant in Dundee.
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair

evidence.text: It was Timex of Portugal, though, that took on the R&D and the local manufacturing of the models to be exported to the U.S. Although both Timex of Scotland and Timex of Portugal were full subsidiaries of Timex, internal rivalry, whether unintended or purported, meant there was little sharing between the two plants.
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair

evidence.text: Timex of Portugal also sold the Timex Sinclair models in Portugal and Poland under the Timex Computer brand.
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair

evidence.text: Sinclair Programs was a magazine published in the United Kingdom, initially by ECC Publications of London and subsequently by EMAP.
evidence.title: Sinclair Programs

evidence.text: It was dedicated entirely to listings for programs for the Sinclair Research ZX80, ZX81 and ZX Spectrum computers, contributed by readers.
evidence.title: Sinclair Programs

evidence.text: The magazine was one of three launched in 1982 by ECC, the other two being "Sinclair User" and "Sinclair Projects", the latter dedicated to hardware projects for the Sinclair computers.
evidence.title: Sinclair Programs

evidence.text: The magazine was published between May/June 1982 and September 1985.
evidence.title: Sinclair Programs

evidence.text: Nigel Searle was the managing director of Sinclair Research Ltd, and one of the company's longest-serving employees.
evidence.title: Nigel Searle

evidence.text: He joined Sinclair Radionics in 1973, and for most of the 1970s, Searle worked for Sinclair in the United States to promote the company's calculators and other products.
evidence.title: Nigel Searle

evidence.text: In 1977, with Sinclair in financial trouble, Searle left the company.
evidence.title: Nigel Searle

evidence.text: He rejoined in 1979 when Sir Clive Sinclair formed Science of Cambridge (later renamed Sinclair Research) and continued to work from the US, successfully promoting the ZX80 and ZX81 personal computers.
evidence.title: Nigel Searle

evidence.text: In spring 1982, he moved back to the United Kingdom as Sinclair's managing director, a post he retained until 1986 when Amstrad took over the company's computer business.
evidence.title: Nigel Searle

evidence.text: Sinclair BASIC is a dialect of the programming language BASIC used in the 8-bit home computers from Sinclair Research and Timex Sinclair.
evidence.title: Sinclair BASIC

evidence.text: The Sinclair BASIC interpreter was made by Nine Tiles Networks Ltd.
evidence.title: Sinclair BASIC

evidence.text: Timex Sinclair was a joint venture between the British company Sinclair Research and Timex Corporation in an effort to gain an entry into the rapidly growing early-1980s home computer market in North America.
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair

evidence.text: The choice of partnership was natural, as Timex was already the main contractor for manufacture of Sinclair's ZX81 and ZX Spectrum computers at its Scottish plant in Dundee.
evidence.title: Timex Sinclair

evidence.text: It was Timex of Portugal, though, that took on the R&D and the local manufacturing of the models to be exported to the U.S. Although both Timex of Scotland and Timex of Portugal were full subsidiaries of Timex, internal rivalry, whether unintended or purported, meant there was little sharing between the two plants.

evidence.text: Sinclair Programs was a magazine published in the United Kingdom, initially by ECC Publications of London and subsequently by EMAP.
evidence.title: Sinclair Programs

evidence.text: It was dedicated entirely to listings for programs for the Sinclair Research ZX80, ZX81 and ZX Spectrum computers, contributed by readers.
evidence.title: Sinclair Programs

evidence.text: The magazine was one of three launched in 1982 by ECC, the other two being "Sinclair User" and "Sinclair Projects", the latter dedicated to hardware projects for the Sinclair computers.
evidence.title: Sinclair Programs

evidence.text: The magazine was published between May/June 1982 and September 1985.

evidence.text: Nigel Searle was the managing director of Sinclair Research Ltd, and one of the company's longest-serving employees.
evidence.title: Nigel Searle

evidence.text: He joined Sinclair Radionics in 1973, and for most of the 1970s, Searle worked for Sinclair in the United States to promote the company's calculators and other products.
evidence.title: Nigel Searle

evidence.text: In 1977, with Sinclair in financial trouble, Searle left the company.
evidence.title: Nigel Searle

evidence.text: He rejoined in 1979 when Sir Clive Sinclair formed Science of Cambridge (later renamed Sinclair Research) and continued to work from the US, successfully promoting the ZX80 and ZX81 personal computers.
evidence.title: Nigel Searle

evidence.text: In spring 1982, he moved back to the United Kingdom as Sinclair's managing director, a post he retained until 1986 when Amstrad took over the company's computer business.
evidence.title: Nigel Searle

evidence.text: The Dali–Ruili Railway or Darui Railway (), is a single-track electrified railroad under construction in Yunnan Province of Southwest China.

evidence.text: The line is slated to run 336.39 km from Dali in central Yunnan to Ruili in southwestern Yunnan on the border with Myanmar.
evidence.title: Dali–Ruili Railway

evidence.text: The line traverses rugged terrain, and bridges and tunnels will account for 75% of the total track length, including a 36-km tunnel through the Gaoligong Mountains.
evidence.title: Dali–Ruili Railway

evidence.text: Construction began in May 2011 and is scheduled to take six years.
evidence.title: Dali–Ruili Railway

evidence.text: Cities and towns along route include Dali, Yangbi Yi Autonomous County, Yongping County, Baoshan, Mang City (also known as Mangshi or Dehong) and Ruili.
evidence.title: Dali–Ruili Railway

evidence.text: The trick film, according to Michael Brooke of BFI Screenonline, "contains one of the first British examples of special effects created by means of jump cuts" Smith employs the jump-cut twice; first to transform his courting couple via "X rays," dramatized by means of the actors donning black bodysuits decorated with skeletons, and then to return them to normal.

evidence.text: The couple in question were played by Smith's wife Laura Bayley and Tom Green (a Brighton comedian).

evidence.text: The String Quartet No. 14 in A-flat major, op.
evidence.title: String Quartet No. 14 (Dvořák)

evidence.text: 105, B. 193, was the last string quartet completed by Antonín Dvořák, even though it was published before his Thirteenth Quartet (which appeared with the higher opus number 106).
evidence.title: String Quartet No. 14 (Dvořák)

evidence.text: Dvořák finished his Fourteenth Quartet in 1895, when he had returned to Bohemia after his visit to America.
evidence.title: String Quartet No. 14 (Dvořák)

evidence.text: The gestation of the Quartet had actually begun in America and lasted six months, which was rather protracted for the composer.
evidence.title: String Quartet No. 14 (Dvořák)

evidence.text: This Quartet marked an important point in Dvořák's development because he would devote himself almost exclusively to writing explicit program music, namely symphonic poems and operas, afterwards.
evidence.title: String Quartet No. 14 (Dvořák)

evidence.text: The Sonatina in G major for violin and piano (), Op.
evidence.title: Violin Sonatina (Dvořák)

evidence.text: 100, B. 183, was written by Antonín Dvořák between November 19 and December 3, 1893, in New York City.
evidence.title: Violin Sonatina (Dvořák)

evidence.text: It was the last chamber composition he wrote during his sojourn in America.
evidence.title: Violin Sonatina (Dvořák)

evidence.text: Dvořák catered the sonatina to the gradually developing musical abilities of his children, especially those of his 15-year-old daughter Ottilie and 10-year-old son Toník.
evidence.title: Violin Sonatina (Dvořák)

evidence.text: In a letter to Fritz Simrock on January 2, 1894, Dvořák conceived the piece in the following terms: ""It is intended for youths (dedicated to my two children), but even grown-ups, adults, should be able to converse with it...""
evidence.title: Violin Sonatina (Dvořák)

evidence.text: The Antonín Dvořák Museum in Prague is a museum dedicated to the great Czech composer Antonín Dvořák (1841-1904).
evidence.title: Antonín Dvořák Museum

evidence.text: Alfred is a heroic opera in three acts by the Czech composer Antonín Dvořák.
evidence.title: Alfred (Dvořák)

evidence.text: It was Dvořák's first opera and the only one he composed to a German text.
evidence.title: Alfred (Dvořák)

evidence.text: The libretto, by Carl Theodor Körner, had already been set by Friedrich von Flotow (as "Alfred der Große") and is based on the story of the English king Alfred the Great.
evidence.title: Alfred (Dvořák)

evidence.text: Composed in 1870, "Alfred" was never performed during Dvořák's lifetime.
evidence.title: Alfred (Dvořák)

evidence.text: It received its premiere (in Czech translation) at the City Theatre, Olomouc on 10 December 1938.
evidence.title: Alfred (Dvořák)

evidence.text: Milada Šubrtová (24 May 1924 – 1 August 2011) was a Czech operatic soprano who had a lengthy career at the National Theatre in Prague from 1948 through 1991.
evidence.title: Milada Šubrtová

evidence.text: She was part of an instrumental group of the post-World War II Czech opera singers that was responsible for popularizing Czech opera internationally.
evidence.title: Milada Šubrtová

evidence.text: She drew particular acclaim for her portrayals of the title heroines in Leoš Janáček's "Jenůfa" and Antonín Dvořák's "Rusalka".
evidence.title: Milada Šubrtová

evidence.text: Mike Long is an American business man, former CEO of several public companies, and currently a founding partner of Sulgrave Partners LLC.
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: He served as the President and Chief Executive Officer of Continuum, an Austin, Texas IT consulting company, from 1991 to 1997, having started with Continuum as a Director in 1983.
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: In 1997, Long was named CEO of Healtheon Corporation (now WebMD), succeeding former CEO David Schnell.
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: Long oversaw Healtheon's initial public offering, traveling between Europe and the United States to woo investors.
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: Long was able to secure the required investment funds, and saw Healtheon's stock price rise from $8 to a high of $120.
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: In 2002, Long was recruited to fix the financial struggles of Move, Inc., a company plagued by more than $4 billion in lawsuits and hemorrhaging tens of millions of dollars a quarter.
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: As Chief Executive Officer, Long was able to revive Homestore, Inc., by changing the business model, rebranding the company as Move, Inc. and returning it to profitability.
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: Touching on his experience of bringing about the initial public offerings of web-based businesses, Long would say that investors needed to be presented "with an entirely new face every few months," and that "the only way to run one of these Silicon Valley companies was to forget everything you'd learned outside of Silicon Valley."
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.title: Sheri McCoy

evidence.text: She was appointed as the Vice Chairman in January 2011, after which she was named by "Fortune Magazine", as the 10th woman on their list of "50 Most Powerful Women in Business", a list on which she has been included since 2008.
evidence.title: Sheri McCoy

evidence.text: In February 2012, she resigned her employment with Johnson & Johnson after 30 years and was subsequently named as the CEO of Avon Products.
evidence.title: Sheri McCoy

evidence.text: In August 2012, she was recognized as the 39th most powerful woman in the world by "Forbes Magazine".
evidence.title: Sheri McCoy

evidence.title: Triple Canopy

evidence.text: The firm was founded in May 2003 by veteran U.S. Army Special Forces Soldiers, including former Delta Operators.
evidence.title: Triple Canopy

evidence.text: In June 2014 the firm merged with rival security contracting firm, Academi, formerly Blackwater, thus forming the new company Constellis Group.
evidence.title: Triple Canopy

evidence.text: The new CEO of Constellis Group is the former CEO of Academi, Craig Nixon, and training facilities are to be consolidated at the existing Academi training facility in North Carolina.
evidence.title: Triple Canopy

evidence.text: It was staffed by, among others, a number of former Army Special Operations personnel, Special Forces Soldiers, Rangers, SEALs, MARSOC Critical Skills Operators, other special operations personnel, and a select few law enforcement officers.
evidence.title: Triple Canopy

evidence.text: Over 5,000 employees worked for Triple Canopy at the time of the merger.
evidence.title: Triple Canopy

evidence.text: Dame Marjorie Morris Scardino, DBE, FRSA (born 25 January 1947) is an American-born British business executive.
evidence.title: Marjorie Scardino

evidence.text: She is the former CEO of Pearson PLC.
evidence.title: Marjorie Scardino

evidence.text: Dame Marjorie became a trustee of Oxfam during her tenure at Pearson .
evidence.title: Marjorie Scardino

evidence.text: Mike Long is an American business man, former CEO of several public companies, and currently a founding partner of Sulgrave Partners LLC.
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: He served as the President and Chief Executive Officer of Continuum, an Austin, Texas IT consulting company, from 1991 to 1997, having started with Continuum as a Director in 1983.
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: In 1997, Long was named CEO of Healtheon Corporation (now WebMD), succeeding former CEO David Schnell.
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: Long oversaw Healtheon's initial public offering, traveling between Europe and the United States to woo investors.
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: Long was able to secure the required investment funds, and saw Healtheon's stock price rise from $8 to a high of $120.
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: In 2002, Long was recruited to fix the financial struggles of Move, Inc., a company plagued by more than $4 billion in lawsuits and hemorrhaging tens of millions of dollars a quarter.
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: As Chief Executive Officer, Long was able to revive Homestore, Inc., by changing the business model, rebranding the company as Move, Inc. and returning it to profitability.
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: Touching on his experience of bringing about the initial public offerings of web-based businesses, Long would say that investors needed to be presented "with an entirely new face every few months," and that "the only way to run one of these Silicon Valley companies was to forget everything you'd learned outside of Silicon Valley."
evidence.title: Mike Long (American businessman)

evidence.text: She was appointed as the Vice Chairman in January 2011, after which she was named by "Fortune Magazine", as the 10th woman on their list of "50 Most Powerful Women in Business", a list on which she has been included since 2008.
evidence.title: Sheri McCoy

evidence.text: In February 2012, she resigned her employment with Johnson & Johnson after 30 years and was subsequently named as the CEO of Avon Products.
evidence.title: Sheri McCoy

evidence.text: In August 2012, she was recognized as the 39th most powerful woman in the world by "Forbes Magazine".
evidence.title: Sheri McCoy

evidence.text: Triple Canopy, Inc., is a private security company that provides integrated security, mission support and risk management services to corporate, government and non-profit clients.
evidence.title: Triple Canopy

evidence.text: The firm was founded in May 2003 by veteran U.S. Army Special Forces Soldiers, including former Delta Operators.
evidence.title: Triple Canopy

evidence.text: In June 2014 the firm merged with rival security contracting firm, Academi, formerly Blackwater, thus forming the new company Constellis Group.
evidence.title: Triple Canopy

evidence.text: The new CEO of Constellis Group is the former CEO of Academi, Craig Nixon, and training facilities are to be consolidated at the existing Academi training facility in North Carolina.
evidence.title: Triple Canopy

evidence.text: It was staffed by, among others, a number of former Army Special Operations personnel, Special Forces Soldiers, Rangers, SEALs, MARSOC Critical Skills Operators, other special operations personnel, and a select few law enforcement officers.
evidence.title: Triple Canopy

evidence.text: Over 5,000 employees worked for Triple Canopy at the time of the merger.
evidence.title: Triple Canopy

evidence.text: Henry Cecil Leon (19 September 1902 – 23 May 1976), who wrote under the pen-names Henry Cecil and Clifford Maxwell, was a judge and a writer of fiction about the British legal system.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: He was born near London in 1902 and was called to the Bar in 1923.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: Later in 1949 he was appointed a County Court Judge, a position he held until 1967.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: He used these experiences as inspiration for his work.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: His books typically feature educated and genteel fraudsters and blackmailers who lay ludicrously ingenious plots exploiting loopholes in the legal system.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: There are several recurring characters, such as the drunken solicitor Mr Tewkesbury and the convoluted and exasperating witness Colonel Brain.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: He writes well about the judicial process, usually through the eyes of a young barrister but sometimes from the viewpoint of the judge; "Friends at Court" contains a memorable snub from a County Court judge to a barrister who is trying to patronise him.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: Cecil did not believe that judges should be too remote from the public: in "Sober as a Judge", a High Court judge, in a case where the ingredients of a martini are of some importance, states drily that he will ignore the convention by which he should inquire "what is a martini?"
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: and instead gives the recipe for the cocktail himself.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.title: Jeanette Winterson

evidence.text: Ike Reilly (born Michael Christopher Reilly) is an American singer-songwriter, musician, and writer as well as frontman and founder of the rock band the Ike Reilly Assassination.
evidence.title: Ike Reilly

evidence.text: He started his music career with various rock bands near his hometown of Libertyville, Illinois, playing guitar for groups such as The Drovers in the late 1980s.
evidence.title: Ike Reilly

evidence.text: After working for a time in music production, in 2001 he released his debut solo album through Universal Records.
evidence.title: Ike Reilly

evidence.text: He afterwards released several albums with The Ike Reilly Assassination, including the well-received "Sparkle in the Finish" in 2004, though Rock Ridge Music.
evidence.title: Ike Reilly

evidence.text: He released his seventh album of solo material, "Born On Fire", in June 2015, as the first album release on Tom Morello's new imprint Firebrand Records.
evidence.title: Ike Reilly

evidence.text: According to Mario Mesquita Borges of Allmusic, "Reilly has followed a trail separate from most of today's singer/songwriters -- unlike other such artists, Reilly prefers the harshness of intrepid rocking riffs, sustained by ingenious melodies and exalting words."
evidence.title: Ike Reilly

evidence.text: Tom Cruise is an American actor and producer who made his film debut with a minor role in the 1981 romantic drama "Endless Love".
evidence.title: Tom Cruise filmography

evidence.title: Tom Cruise filmography

evidence.text: In 1986, Cruise played a fighter pilot in the Tony Scott-directed action drama "Top Gun" (the highest-grossing film that year), and also starred opposite Paul Newman in the Martin Scorsese-directed drama "The Color of Money".
evidence.title: Tom Cruise filmography

evidence.text: Two years later he played opposite Dustin Hoffman in the Academy Award for Best Picture-winning drama "Rain Man" (1988), and also appeared in the Golden Raspberry Award for Worst Picture-winning romantic drama "Cocktail" (1988).
evidence.title: Tom Cruise filmography

evidence.text: In doing so Cruise became the first and only person as of 2014 to star in a Best Picture Oscar winner and a Worst Picture Razzie winner in the same year.
evidence.title: Tom Cruise filmography

evidence.text: His next role was as anti-war activist Ron Kovic in the drama adaptation of Kovic's memoir of the same name, "Born on the Fourth of July" (1989).
evidence.title: Tom Cruise filmography

evidence.text: For his performance Cruise received the Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Motion Picture Drama and his first nomination for the Academy Award for Best Actor.
evidence.title: Tom Cruise filmography

evidence.text: Henry Cecil Leon (19 September 1902 – 23 May 1976), who wrote under the pen-names Henry Cecil and Clifford Maxwell, was a judge and a writer of fiction about the British legal system.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: He was born near London in 1902 and was called to the Bar in 1923.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: Later in 1949 he was appointed a County Court Judge, a position he held until 1967.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: He used these experiences as inspiration for his work.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: His books typically feature educated and genteel fraudsters and blackmailers who lay ludicrously ingenious plots exploiting loopholes in the legal system.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: There are several recurring characters, such as the drunken solicitor Mr Tewkesbury and the convoluted and exasperating witness Colonel Brain.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: He writes well about the judicial process, usually through the eyes of a young barrister but sometimes from the viewpoint of the judge; "Friends at Court" contains a memorable snub from a County Court judge to a barrister who is trying to patronise him.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: Cecil did not believe that judges should be too remote from the public: in "Sober as a Judge", a High Court judge, in a case where the ingredients of a martini are of some importance, states drily that he will ignore the convention by which he should inquire "what is a martini?"
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon

evidence.text: and instead gives the recipe for the cocktail himself.
evidence.title: Henry Cecil Leon
